prize_parts.citation: for the development of targeted protein degradation, in which small molecules such as PROTACs and molecular glues direct the ubiquitin-proteasome system to eliminate chosen proteins

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B063 as a single-part prize to Crews, Deshaies and Handa. Targeted protein degradation is a new chemical modality in which a small molecule does not occupy a protein but recruits the cell's own ubiquitin ligase machinery to remove it. The chemistry is explicit and testable: ligand and linker design, ternary-complex cooperativity, and cereblon as the target through which thalidomide-class molecular glues act. Having read the full first round, I find the three supporters (Aili, Linke and I) converge on the same names and on the same split of credit, with a concept strand (Crews and Deshaies, who conceived and demonstrated PROTACs) and a mechanism strand (Handa, who identified cereblon). Linke's argument that this division yields a defensible three-person set persuades me more than breadth of opening support does. Every member ranked B063 in the opening, but I now rest my position on the mechanism, the independent reproduction in many laboratories, and the fact that acute chemical removal of a protein has become an everyday tool for biochemists, including those who study the nucleotide-metabolism enzymes I work on.
statement.case_against: The main reservation is still clinical maturity, since no degrader is approved. I weigh it as a timing question and not a question of merit, because the Nobel Prize in Chemistry has recognised methods whose scientific content was settled before every application was realised, and the protein-removal mechanism is established regardless of any single trial. I accept that this argument weakens if early clinical readouts turn sour or if resistance through E3 ligase loss proves severe. Attribution remains the second weakness. Ciulli (VHL ligands and the structural basis of ternary complexes), Ito, Gray, Sakamoto and Kim all have substantive claims, and the chair is right that the three-person limit forces an exclusion. I do not have a better cut. Replacing Deshaies with Ciulli would trade the conceptual origin of PROTACs for the structure-guided chemistry, and I judge the origin to carry more weight. The citation may also be read as joining two historically distinct strands, and I accept that risk. Lastly, my biochemical background may tilt me toward chemical-biology candidates.

responses.point: Linke moved B063 from fourth to first because the credit divides cleanly into a concept strand (Crews and Deshaies) and a mechanism strand (Handa), and he asks whether Deshaies, Ciulli or Ito should displace a name; he also concedes that breadth of ranking is not evidence of merit and that the choice would look premature if approvals slip.
responses.response: I agree with the strand argument and it is the reason I keep the same three names. On the chair's question of whom to displace, I would not displace anyone. Ito's cereblon work is a co-discovery with Handa, but Handa's identification of the thalidomide target and the follow-up on its substrate-recruiting mechanism carry the decisive credit. Ciulli's contribution is real but sits on the optimisation side of a concept already demonstrated by Crews and Deshaies. I share his caution about breadth of support. As to what evidence would suffice, I would not require an approved drug. Reproducible acute degradation in many laboratories and early human proof-of-concept already meet the standard of validated chemistry, and approval would add comfort without changing the science.

responses.point: Sparr prefers ionizable lipid nanoparticles (B035) with Cullis, Hope and Madden, arguing that the 2023 Medicine prize recognised the cargo and not the carrier, that the pKa-tuned lipid and assembly principle is clean chemistry, and that the primary literature rather than patent history should decide the names.
responses.response: I agree that her chemical argument is strong and that maturity is beyond doubt for B035, which is why it remains my first alternative. Her point on relying on the primary literature is fair, and I withdraw my earlier leaning on the patent history. My difficulty is different. I still cannot see how to settle the names when Anderson's lipidoids and MacLachlan's clinical translation are independent routes to the same carrier chemistry, and when she herself concedes that the credit is debatable. In B063 the three names are named by three members and are not contested on priority. I also note that she lists B063 as an alternative, so we may not differ on whether the two candidates are prize-worthy but only on which has the cleaner credit.

responses.point: Aqvist proposes a two-part prize pairing ionizable lipid nanoparticles (Cullis, Anderson) with base editing (Liu alone), and states that B063 has the broadest opening support and arguably the most chemical novelty and ranks behind his choices only because of attribution and clinical maturity.
responses.response: His concession that B063 has the most chemical novelty is the central point, and I am glad he named his reasons for ranking it lower so that I can address them. On clinical maturity I would say that his own base editing part is under a decade old with long-term safety open, so that criterion does not clearly favour his configuration over mine. On attribution, B063 is supported by three members on the same names, whereas his lipid part pairs Cullis with Anderson, a pairing his colleague Sparr contests. I also resist the two-part form. Joining a delivery chemistry and a genome-editing chemistry gives two prizes at a stage when neither has a settled credit, and a single clearly defined achievement seems stronger.

responses.point: Brzezinski prefers proton-coupled electron transfer (B025) as a physical principle with decades of confirmation, and admits that it reads as a broad field, that T. J. Meyer's work complicates a three-person cut, and that B063 has more support and a more obvious pharmacological payoff.
responses.response: His candour about B025 counts for a great deal with me. A unifying principle confirmed over decades is the kind of discovery the prize has honoured, and I do not regard it as lesser science. In my first-round response I asked whether he could support B063 if B025 does not gain traction, and he has partly answered that by listing it as his first alternative and by granting that it is the crisp, widely visible achievement. I would ask him to weigh that, given that he himself says the attribution of B025 is awkward because of Meyer. I accept his earlier point that B063 is less mature, but I think the mechanistic content makes the case sufficient without waiting for an approval.

uncertainties: Whether PROTACs and cereblon-mediated molecular glues will be read as one discovery or as two strands joined awkwardly, and whether a narrower citation would be safer
Whether the absence of an approved degrader will still look like a reasonable timing decision if early clinical signals prove disappointing
Whether leaving out Ciulli, Ito, Gray, Sakamoto and Kim is defensible, since the three-person limit forces an exclusion that I cannot make cleaner
Whether B035, if its credit could be settled, should take precedence over B063 for a committee that weighs maturity above conceptual novelty
statement.conflict_note: No conflict or recusal is needed, and I have nothing to add to my earlier disclosure. My work on nucleotide metabolism and replication fidelity does not overlap with any shortlisted candidate, and I have no documented collaboration with any credited person. I note only that I am a biologist-classified academician with a biochemistry background, so I may be biased toward chemical-biology candidates such as B063, and I have weighed that in this position.
